title: LexisNexis Launches Next Evolution of Lexis+ with Protégé, the Legal AI Platform Built on the Authority Legal Work Demands
author: LexisNexis Legal & Professional

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: LexisNexis accepts the cluster’s emphasis on verification and use-context-specific governance, and materially extends it with concrete workflow controls: source-linked outputs, automated citation checking, permission-aware collaboration, audit trails and customer-controlled encryption. These are product-capability claims rather than independent evidence of realised organisational value or general legal competence.
qs: **Shepard's® Verify Trust Markers bring LexisNexis's trusted citation authority directly into AI-assisted work.** The capability identifies legal citations in AI-generated and attorney-drafted content, checks them against LexisNexis authoritative legal sources, and flags citations that cannot be verified as existing.
Outputs link back to source material including exact document passages, spreadsheet rows, images or timestamps so legal teams can verify findings and defend the work product that follows.

st.t: Legal platforms: Content and governance differentiate workflows
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition that legal-AI differentiation comes from authoritative content, integrated workflows, model flexibility, security and governance rather than models alone. It also preserves lawyer oversight by describing visible, controlled execution that produces review-ready—not independently reliable—work. Its benefit claims remain vendor assertions without measured or independent validation.
qs: "They need one trusted environment where authoritative content, firm knowledge, advanced models, legal workflows and security controls work together.
Instead of generating a single response, Protégé presents a structured plan for the work, giving users visibility and control as it executes tasks and produces review-ready legal work product.

kp.k: Legal AI requires authority, verification and governance
kp.d: The release argues that generating text and automating isolated tasks are insufficient for legal practice: legal AI also requires authoritative content, verification tools, matter-file integration and confidentiality governance. LexisNexis frames invented citations, unsupported conclusions, inconsistent drafting and uncontrolled matter data as risks of AI lacking these safeguards. These are the vendor's arguments for an integrated platform, rather than reported comparative findings.
qs: But legal work requires something more demanding: current, authoritative legal content; verification tools; a connection to files; governance for confidentiality and privilege; and workflows that reflect how lawyers practice.

AI without deep legal authority and built-in verification may accelerate work, but it can also accelerate risk from invented citations and unsupported conclusions to inconsistent drafting, uncontrolled matter data and weak auditability.

kp.k: Agentic workflows organize multi-step legal work
kp.d: LexisNexis describes Protégé Work as moving beyond single-response generation: users select a skill or state a goal, and the system routes requests, presents a structured plan and executes tasks with user visibility and control. Listed applications include contract comparison, complaint analysis, research synthesis, due diligence and compliance review. The vendor claims reusable workflows support consistent firm and department standards; skills include LexisNexis-developed and Anthropic-powered capabilities, with further additions planned.
qs: Users can select a skill directly or describe a legal goal in natural language.
Instead of generating a single response, Protégé presents a structured plan for the work, giving users visibility and control as it executes tasks and produces review-ready legal work product.
Skills support repeatable tasks such as contract comparison, complaint analysis, research synthesis, checklist generation, due diligence, compliance review and playbook-based review.
Lexis+ with Protégé incorporates LexisNexis-developed and Anthropic-powered skills, with additional skills and capabilities planned over time.

kp.k: Drafting agents produce review-ready, organization-specific documents
kp.d: The release claims drafting agents can produce review-ready contracts, motions, briefs and deal documents in minutes using legal content, templates, prior work and matter materials. Drafts can incorporate organizational style and exemplars, preserve formatting and surface risks before external delivery. The stated output is review-ready rather than a substitute for lawyer review; the release supplies no measured drafting-time comparison.
qs: Protégé Agentic Drafting helps lawyers and legal teams produce review-ready work product in minutes.
Purpose-built drafting agents create contracts, motions, briefs and deal documents grounded in LexisNexis content, firm templates, prior work and matter materials.
Drafts can reflect an organization's preferred style, apply vetted exemplars, preserve formatting and surface risk considerations before work reaches a client, counterparty or court.

kp.k: AI outputs integrate with everyday legal document formats
kp.d: The release describes delivering skill outputs in established office formats, linking AI workflows to drafting, structured review and client communications rather than limiting outputs to conversational responses.
qs: This includes Microsoft Word for drafts, Excel for review tables and structured findings, PowerPoint for client-ready summaries, and PDF for polished, ready-to-use work product.

kp.k: Permission controls support collaboration across organizational boundaries
kp.d: LexisNexis presents Workrooms as shared spaces for law firms, corporate legal departments and counsel to collaborate on documents, analysis and AI workflows. It identifies dual approvals, least-privilege access, role-based permissions and audit trails as controls intended to preserve confidentiality while enabling cross-organizational work.
qs: Law firms, corporate legal departments and counsel can work together in private, permission-aware spaces where documents, drafts, analysis and AI workflows are shared only as authorized.
Dual approvals, least-privilege access, role-based permissions and audit trails help teams collaborate across organizational lines while maintaining control of confidential information.

kp.k: Citation checks target authority existence and retrievability
kp.d: Shepard's Verify is described as identifying citations in both AI-generated and attorney-drafted content, checking them against LexisNexis sources and flagging unverified citations. The stated function confirms existence and retrievability; the release does not describe this capability as establishing that cited authority supports a particular legal conclusion. LexisNexis claims it helps protect professional reputation and increases confidence when finalizing work.
qs: The capability identifies legal citations in AI-generated and attorney-drafted content, checks them against LexisNexis authoritative legal sources, and flags citations that cannot be verified as existing.

By confirming that cited authority exists and is retrievable at the point of use, Shepard's Verify helps legal professionals protect their professional reputation and move from draft to final with greater confidence.

kp.k: Large-matter analysis links findings to underlying sources
kp.d: The redesigned Vault reportedly supports up to 100,000 documents per Vault across documents, spreadsheets, images, audio, video and other materials. Outputs link to precise passages, rows, images or timestamps so legal teams can check findings against matter evidence and defend resulting work product.
qs: Teams can analyze documents, PDFs, spreadsheets, images, audio, video and other matter materials in one workspace, with support for up to 100,000 documents per Vault.
Outputs link back to source material including exact document passages, spreadsheet rows, images or timestamps so legal teams can verify findings and defend the work product that follows.

kp.d: The release describes Bring Your Own Key encryption for enterprise and government customers, allowing customer management of encryption keys and revocation of access. It states that all customer data at rest is encrypted through the customer's key-management service and reports deployment in AmLaw 100 firms after extensive testing, without naming firms or providing testing results.
qs: With Bring Your Own Key encryption, customers can manage their own encryption keys through their chosen key management service and revoke access when required, supporting the data-control expectations of law firms, regulated industries and public-sector legal teams.

With BYOK, LexisNexis integrates directly with a customer's own Key Management Service (KMS) — including AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, Google Cloud KMS, and HashiCorp Vault — to encrypt all customer data at rest using keys that only the customer controls.
After extensive testing, BYOK has been deployed in AmLaw 100 firms.

kp.k: Vendor claims efficiency gains and plans global rollout
kp.d: The 7 May 2026 announcement claims faster research and drafting, stronger initial drafts, more consistent standards, reduced citation and review risk, and improved matter handling and collaboration. These are vendor assertions without quantified outcome evidence in the release. Following the US launch, LexisNexis states that global rollout will occur throughout 2026.
qs: For customers, the result is practical and immediate: faster research and drafting cycles, stronger first drafts, more consistent application of firm and client standards, reduced citation and review risk, better handling of large matter files, and more secure collaboration between legal teams and clients.
Following its US launch, the new and evolved Lexis+ with Protégé legal AI platform — for automating complex legal work — will be rolled out globally throughout 2026.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: LexisNexis claims that integrated legal AI can accelerate complex legal work while improving accuracy, consistency and control, whereas AI without legal authority and verification can accelerate legal and information-governance risks.
pts.d: The corporate press release attributes the claimed benefits to integrating authoritative legal content, Shepard's intelligence, customer knowledge, workflows and security. CEO Sean Fitzpatrick frames scalable legal AI as producing work lawyers can verify and defend, rather than merely plausible answers. These are claims about augmentation of legal professionals, not autonomous replacement of lawyers.

pts.k: LexisNexis claims agentic workflows shift AI use from single responses to planned task execution, and drafting agents produce review-ready legal documents in minutes.
pts.d: Protégé Work reportedly routes user-selected skills or natural-language goals into structured workflows with user visibility and control. Claimed applications include contract comparison, complaint analysis, research synthesis, due diligence, compliance and playbook-based review. Drafting agents reportedly use legal content, templates, prior work and matter materials to produce contracts, motions, briefs and deal documents that reflect organizational standards. The release describes outputs as review-ready, not as eliminating human review, and says outputs can be delivered in Word, Excel, PowerPoint and PDF.

pts.k: LexisNexis claims citation checking and source-linked matter analysis make AI-assisted work easier to verify and defend.
pts.d: Shepard's Verify Trust Markers reportedly identify citations in both AI-generated and attorney-drafted content, check them against LexisNexis sources and flag citations that cannot be verified as existing. The stated check establishes existence and retrievability; the release does not say it establishes that every citation supports the associated proposition. Protégé Vault reportedly analyzes multimodal matter materials, supports up to 100,000 documents per Vault and links outputs to specific underlying sources so legal teams can check findings.

pts.k: LexisNexis claims permission-controlled collaboration and customer-controlled encryption enable legal teams to use AI across organizational boundaries while retaining control of confidential data.
pts.d: Protégé Workrooms reportedly provide private shared spaces for documents, drafts, analysis and workflows. The release links dual approvals, least-privilege access, role-based permissions and audit trails to confidential collaboration. Protégé BYOK reportedly lets customers control encryption keys through their own key management service and revoke access when required. The claimed outcome is more secure collaboration and additional control for enterprise and government users.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The offered basis is vendor-described functionality, reliance on LexisNexis legal authority, executive statements and a report of BYOK testing and deployment; no quantified outcome study or comparative benchmark is supplied.
pts.d: The release explains mechanisms intended to deliver its benefits: authoritative content, reusable workflows, source links, citation-existence checks and security controls. It gives a document-capacity specification and an unbenchmarked claim that drafting takes minutes. It reports extensive BYOK testing and deployment in AmLaw 100 firms but supplies no testing methods, named firms, sample sizes or results. It provides no measured improvements in accuracy, drafting quality, review risk or cycle times. Sean Fitzpatrick's statements are executive assertions rather than independent validation.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 7 May 2026 release presents benefits as immediate, claims drafting in minutes, and predicts global rollout throughout 2026 following the US launch.
pts.d: The announced functionality is presented as the current platform expansion; further skills and capabilities are planned without specific dates. BYOK deployment in AmLaw 100 firms is described as already completed after testing. Benefits are tied to use of the platform's integrated content, organizational knowledge, verification features and governance controls. Workflows retain user visibility and control and produce review-ready work, qualifying the extent of automation.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed effects primarily concern law firms, corporate legal departments and their clients, with additional data-control benefits for enterprise, regulated-industry and public-sector legal teams.
pts.d: Lawyers and legal teams are positioned as users of faster research, drafting, review and large-matter analysis, while retaining responsibility for checking and defending work. Firms and corporate legal departments reportedly gain more consistent application of organizational and client standards and more secure collaboration with each other and clients. AmLaw 100 firms are specifically identified as BYOK adopters. Clients, counterparties and courts are downstream recipients before whom drafting risks may be surfaced. The release does not predict lawyer job losses, staffing changes, fee reductions or improved access to justice.
